query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing fixed EAM reference potentials with an actively‐trained machine learning interatomic potential—such as an error‐controlled moment tensor potential or deep neural network potential—will better capture the diverse atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid in multicomponent high‐entropy alloys, thereby improving the reference–target phase-space overlap and reducing the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys (e.g., refractory systems containing elements such as W, Ta, Mo, etc.) in both solid and liquid states at temperatures at or very near their high melting points (typically above 1850°C).
generation.intervention: Implement a module that actively learns from ab initio high-temperature liquid configurations to train a machine learning potential (e.g., moment tensor potential or DNN potential) and use it as the reference in thermodynamic integration.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions at and near the melting point (approximately 3000–3500 K) for refractory high-entropy alloy compositions.
generation.structural_mediator: An ML potential framework that dynamically samples the local atomic arrangements in the liquid, capturing structural heterogeneities that fixed EAM potentials ignore.
generation.mechanism: The ML potential, by training on diverse liquid configurations, more accurately maps the complex energy landscape encountered in the ab initio liquid. This enhanced representation improves phase-space overlap between the reference and target systems, resulting in reduced integration path mismatches and lower cumulative free-energy errors during thermodynamic integration.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in the thermodynamic-integration path mismatch compared to the TOR-TILD method, with a predicted uncertainty reduction that may lower free-energy integration errors by on the order of (tentatively) ~50%. Exact values remain uncertain until benchmarked against ab initio results.
generation.baseline: Free-energy calculations performed using TOR-TILD’s conventional EAM references under identical high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This approach is applicable to high-melting refractory, multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their melting temperature. Its performance for systems with substantially different chemical compositions, lower temperatures, or different structural regimes remains to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in integration path mismatch is uncertain and will depend on the quality and transferability of the ML training data. The approach might encounter challenges if the sampling of rare liquid configurations is incomplete.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of free-energy integration calculations on a representative high-melting high-entropy alloy using both the conventional TOR-TILD EAM references and the new ML potential. The experiment should involve high-temperature simulations (around 3000–3500 K) and cover both solid and liquid phases. Compare the integration path mismatches and convergence behavior with ab initio benchmark calculations.
measurements: Thermodynamic-integration path mismatch (quantified as the difference in free-energy integration error between reference and target states)
Absolute free-energy differences compared to ab initio benchmarks
Convergence rates of the integration paths
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML potential fails to demonstrate a statistically significant decrease in integration path mismatch (i.e. free-energy errors are not reduced by a measurable margin compared to outputs from TOR-TILD’s EAM references) or exhibits convergence behavior that does not surpass that of the EAM approach under identical conditions, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

## Abstract
While first-principles methods have been successfully applied to characterize individual properties of multi-principal element alloys (MPEA), their use in searching for optimal trade-offs between competing properties is hampered by high computational demands. In this work, we present a framework to explore Pareto-optimal compositions by integrating advanced ab initio-based techniques into a Bayesian multi-objective optimization workflow, complemented by a simple analytical model providing straightforward analysis of trends. We benchmark the framework by applying it to solid solution strengthening and ductility of refractory MPEAs, with the parameters of the strengthening and ductility models being efficiently computed using a combination of the coherent-potential approximation method, accounting for finite-temperature effects, and actively-learned moment-tensor potentials parameterized with ab initio data. Properties obtained from ab initio calculations are subsequently used to extend predictions of all relevant material properties to a large class of refractory alloys with the help of the analytical model validated by the data and relying on a few element-specific para

## Abstract
The melting temperature is a crucial property of materials that determines their potential applications in different industrial fields. In this study, we used a deep neural network potential to describe the structure of high-entropy (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x carbonitrides (HECN) in both solid and liquid states. This approach allows us to predict heating and cooling temperatures depending on the nitrogen content to determine the melting temperature and analyze structure changes from atomistic point of view. A steady increase in nitrogen content leads to increasing melting temperature, with a maximum approaching for 25% of nitrogen in the HECN. A careful analysis of pair correlations, together with calculations of entropy in the considered liquid phases of HECNs allows us to explain the origin of the nonlinear enhancement of the melting temperature with increasing nitrogen content. The maximum melting temperature of 3580 ± 30 K belongs to (TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25 composition. The improved melting behavior of high-entropy compounds by the addition of nitrogen provides a promising way towards modification of thermal properties of functional and constructional materials.
